title: Battery capacity tester (constant-current load)
summary: Build a constant-current load with automatic cut-off from an op-amp, a TL431, a MOSFET and a shunt resistor. It drains a cell or battery at a set current until it reaches its empty voltage, and a clock that stops at the same moment tells you how long it lasted. Amps × hours = capacity.

materials.item: N-channel MOSFET 30V+, 10A+, in a big case (TO-220 or larger)
Heatsink with fan (CPU cooler for loads over 10W)
Resistors: a 0.1–1 Ω 1–5W shunt, plus 1 kΩ, 4.7 kΩ, 10 kΩ and 40 kΩ (or 39 kΩ)
12V relay, DPDT, contacts rated above your test current
NPN transistor to drive the relay
Fuse in the positive lead of the battery under test, about 1.5× the test current (2–10A)
Clips or holders for the battery under test

steps.text: Plan your current and power. MOSFET heat = battery volts × current. A Li-ion cell at 1A is about 4W; a 12V battery at 2A is about 25W and needs a CPU cooler with its fan running.

Build the current regulator (op-amp A, see notes): TL431 makes 2.5V, a pot divides it down to the set voltage, the op-amp drives the MOSFET gate so the shunt voltage equals the set voltage. Current = set voltage ÷ shunt ohms.

Build the cut-off (op-amp B): it compares the battery voltage, through a 4:1 divider, with a second pot. Its output drives the transistor and relay. The relay's first contact connects the battery to the load.
Wire the start button across that relay contact. Put a 10 kΩ resistor from the switched battery line to ground so the cut-off sees 0V once the relay opens; this latches it off.
Wire the relay's second contact into one battery lead of the quartz clock, so the clock runs only while the test runs.
Mount the MOSFET on the heatsink with thermal paste. Keep the shunt and the battery leads short and thick.
steps.warn: The heatsink and shunt get hot enough to burn. Keep them clear of anything flammable.

steps.text: Set up with a bench supply or a known battery: set the cut-off voltage (3.0V for Li-ion, 1.0V per cell for NiMH, 10.5V for a 12V lead-acid), then set the current by reading the voltage across the shunt.
Fit the fuse in the battery-under-test positive lead, right at the clip. Mark the clips + and − clearly and check polarity with the meter every time before pressing start.
steps.warn: Connected backwards, the MOSFET's built-in diode shorts the battery through the shunt. Without the fuse, wires and shunt can burn.

steps.text: Test: connect a fully charged battery, set the clock to 12:00, press start. The relay pulls in and the clock runs. When the battery reaches the cut-off, the relay drops out and the clock stops.
steps.warn: Watch lithium cells during tests. Stop at once if a cell gets hot, swells or hisses, and move it onto sand or bare earth.

steps.text: Capacity = current × hours on the clock. Example: 1.0A for 2 h 12 min = 2.2Ah (2,200 mAh). Write it on the cell or battery.
Recharge lead-acid batteries straight after a test; leaving them flat damages them.
steps.warn: Old batteries can leak acid. Wear eye protection, and recharge in a ventilated space away from sparks.

notes:
## Circuit
**Supply:** 9–12V to the op-amp (pin 8 +, pin 4 −) and the relay. The battery under test shares the circuit's ground (its negative).

**Reference:** 1 kΩ from +12V to TL431 cathode; cathode and reference pins joined; anode to ground. That gives 2.5V.

**Op-amp A (current):** 2.5V → 10 kΩ pot to ground. Pot wiper → 40 kΩ (or 39 kΩ) → + input, with 4.7 kΩ from + input to ground, giving 0–0.26V. Output → 1 kΩ → MOSFET gate. − input → 1 kΩ → MOSFET source (top of shunt). Shunt from source to ground. MOSFET drain → switched battery +.
- With a 0.1 Ω shunt: 0.1V = 1A, up to about 2.6A.
- With a 1 Ω shunt: 0.1V = 100 mA, for small cells.
- Shunt heat = current² × ohms: 2A in 0.1 Ω = 0.4W.

**Op-amp B (cut-off):** switched battery + → 40 kΩ → + input, 10 kΩ from + input to ground (divides by 5). 2.5V → second 10 kΩ pot → wiper to − input. Output → 4.7 kΩ → NPN base, emitter to ground, collector to relay coil, coil top to +12V, diode across the coil.
- Threshold at the − input = cut-off voltage ÷ 5: 3.0V → 0.60V; 10.5V → 2.10V.
- The pot gives thresholds up to 2.5V, so cut-offs from about 0.5V to 12.5V can be set.

**Latch:** battery + → relay contact 1 → switched battery line. 10 kΩ from the switched line to ground. Start button across contact 1. Pressing start feeds battery voltage to the cut-off, the relay pulls in and holds itself. When the battery sags to the cut-off, the relay opens, the switched line drops to 0V and it stays off even when the battery voltage recovers.

## Settings
| Battery | Cut-off | Test current |
|---|---|---|
| Li-ion cell | 3.0V | 0.5–1A |
| NiMH AA | 1.0V | 0.2–0.5A |
| 12V lead-acid | 10.5V | capacity ÷ 20 (5A for 100Ah) |
| 12V 7Ah alarm battery | 10.5V | 0.35A |

Lead-acid capacity is rated at a 20-hour rate. Testing faster gives a lower number.

## Heat limits
A MOSFET used as a linear load must shed all the power as heat. Stay under about 20–30W per device with a CPU cooler and fan; split bigger loads across two MOSFETs, each with its own shunt and op-amp section.

## No electronics version
Put a power resistor or a 12V bulb across the battery, measure volts and current every 15–30 minutes and write them down with the time. Stop at the cut-off voltage. Capacity ≈ average current × hours. A 55W headlight bulb draws about 4.5A from a 12V battery.

## Troubleshooting
- Current wanders up and down: add 100 nF from the op-amp output to its − input, and keep the shunt leads short.
- Relay chatters at cut-off: the 10 kΩ pull-down is missing, so the line floats.
- Can't reach the set current: battery voltage too low for the shunt plus MOSFET drop, or the gate voltage too low; use a logic-level MOSFET for low-voltage cells.
